land.text: Singapore island, which Parameswara left in 1398 and which Malacca later 'absorbed' as a Laksamana's fiefdom (undated); nothing passed in 1400

predecessors.note: No land passed at the founding: Parameswara 'fled to the west coast of the Malay Peninsula to establish the Malacca Sultanate in 1400' (Kingdom of Singapura page), so the link is the founder and his line. The island was absorbed into Malacca's realm at an undated later time; the Singapura dossier lists Malacca as its successor with the same island.

land.text: the south of the peninsula by the Johor River, where Alauddin Riayat Shah II 'established a new capital' in 1528 (Johor Sultanate page: 'founded in 1528 ... based at Pekan Tua')

successors.note: Alauddin Riayat Shah II founded Johor in 1528 (Johor Sultanate page: 'founded in 1528'). The exile court held only Kampar in 1526-1528 (the Capture page), so the Johor heartland came to the heir as a dynastic claim, not as land the sultanate still held; the Riau islands (Bintan was razed and returned to its previous ruler in 1526) and the Sumatran coast came to Johor later, 'at its height' (Johor page), and are not drawn as handed over in 1528.

land.text: the north of the peninsula, where Muzaffar Shah 'was invited to rule'

successors.note: The Perak page gives no founding year; the Malacca page puts the partition into Johor and Perak in 1528.

capitals.name: Malacca (Melaka)
capitals.note: Infobox 'Malacca (1400-1511)'; the city fell in August 1511.

capitals.name: Muar River mouth (camp)
capitals.note: After the fall 'the sultan retreated a few kilometers south of Malacca, to the mouth of the Muar River'; the Portuguese forced him out of the camp (May, after Albuquerque left in January 1512), and he went to Pahang. The Malacca infobox dates Bintan from 1511; the Capture text puts the Muar camp and Pahang first. Coordinates are Muar town, approximate.

capitals.name: Bintan
capitals.note: Infobox 'Bintan (1511-1526)'; Mahmud 'moved to Bintan, an island kingdom ... that he usurped to wage war on the Portuguese' until they 'devastated Bintan in 1526'. The year of the move is not on any page: 1513 is the researcher's reading (a year in Pahang after the camp was lost in 1512). Coordinates are the island's north-west coast, approximate.

capitals.name: Kampar (Sumatra)
capitals.note: Infobox 'Kampar (1526-1528)': the last capital, where Mahmud Shah died. Coordinates are Bangkinang, the Kampar regency seat, approximate.

rulers.name: Mansur Shah
rulers.note: the Mansur Shah page's infobox says 1456-1477, its text 1459-1477

rulers.name: Mahmud Shah
rulers.note: first reign; the city fell in August 1511

rulers.name: Mahmud Shah
rulers.note: second reign, in exile at Bintan and Kampar; died 1528 (Malacca and Perak pages) or 1527 (Capture of Malacca page)

correction.text: the port Parameswara founded on the west coast of the Malay Peninsula c. 1400

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria's first row begins in 1459, fifty-nine years after the founding (infobox 'c. 1400'). The page gives no area; the early realm was the port and its river mouth until the reign of Megat Iskandar Shah (1414-1424).

correction.text: the coast 'from Kuala Linggi to Kuala Kesang', roughly the modern state of Malacca

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 1424-1458. Pahang is added by the 1454 conquest and the Dindings-to-Johor coast by Muzaffar Shah's reign (1446-1459); both are ledger events, so this keyframe is the core only.

correction.text: the realm at Mansur Shah's accession: Malacca's coast, 'the territory between the Dindings and Johor' (Muzaffar Shah), and Pahang (conquered 1454)

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria's 6,939 km2 shape (bbox 103.0-104.2 E, 0.9-1.8 N) lies on Singapore, south Johor and the Riau islands and does not contain Malacca town (102.25 E, 2.19 N); 94 percent of its cells lie inside Cliopatria's Majapahit shape. The infobox gives no area. The page: Muzaffar Shah 'was the first Malaccan ruler to hold authority over both ends of the peninsula'. Sumatran gains (1477), Riau-Lingga (1488) and Kelantan (1506) come as ledger events on top of this shape. Pahang is direct land only to 1470 (the ledger takes it out as a vassal sultanate from 1470 to 1511, Pahang Sultanate page).

correction.text: the sultan's camp 'at the mouth of the Muar River', his last ground in Malacca's hinterland until the Portuguese drove him out in 1512

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria's 230,357 km2 shape (99.8-104.9 E, 2.4 S-6.3 N) keeps the whole peninsula and central Sumatra for the exile court; the Capture page's infobox says the opposite: 'Destruction of the Malacca Sultanate; independence of Kampar, Pahang, and others'. The page names the troops sent in 1511 (Palembang, Indragiri, Menangkabau, Pahang) but no province that stayed Malaccan afterwards, and the Malacca page says the former vassals 'were no longer paying homage' to him. So the shape is what the page places the sultan on: the Muar camp (to 1512), then Bintan (next keyframe), then Kampar. Pahang gave him refuge for about a year (Pahang page) without being his land. The 230,357 km2 is dropped (verdict wrong).

correction.text: Bintan, 'an island kingdom south-east of Singapore that he usurped to wage war on the Portuguese in Malacca'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. The exile court's seat and only land while it raided Portuguese Malacca; the Portuguese 'devastated Bintan in 1526, returning it to its previous ruler and vassalizing the kingdom'. The pages give neither the year of the move (1513 is the researcher's reading) nor any other island or province under the sultan; whether the Riau-Lingga islands conquered in 1488 stayed loyal is not stated, so they are not drawn. The 35 km radius is a coarse stand-in for the island.

correction.text: Kampar in Sumatra, where Mahmud Shah 'led a government-in-exile there until he died'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. After Bintan fell in 1526 Mahmud Shah 'retreated to Kampar, Sumatra' (Capture page; the Malacca infobox lists Kampar 1526-1528 as capital). The page says Kampar had been the 'only renegade state' in 1511, so this is a refuge whose terms the pages do not give. Kampar is not in the gazetteer: radius round Bangkinang, approximate.

The sultanate was partitioned in 1528 ('The Malacca Sultanate ... partition 1528, into the Johor and Perak sultanates'); Perak and Johor have their own rows from 1529. The town of Malacca itself was Portuguese ('130 years from 1511 to 1641').

The row continues 111 years past the end of the sultanate.

The Dutch took the town in January 1641 ('captured the city in January 1641'); it was a 'Colony of the Dutch East India Company' 1641-1795.

region.text: the stronghold on the west coast of the Malay Peninsula

ledger.note: c. 1400: Parameswara, driven from Singapura, founds Malacca. Infobox 'Founding: c. 1400'; the Kingdom of Singapura page: 'Parameswara, fled to the west coast of the Malay Peninsula to establish the Malacca Sultanate in 1400'. The page says earlier dates have been proposed.

region.text: Malacca's tributary relation to the Ming; the relation is Malacca's, no Chinese land

ledger.note: 1405: the Ming open tributary relations with Malacca. 'In 1405, the Yongle Emperor ... sent his envoy headed by Yin Qing to Malacca'; 'In exchange for regular tribute, the Chinese emperor offered Malacca protection from the constant threat of Siamese attack' (undated). The Megat Iskandar Shah page: tribute to the Yongle Emperor in 1414. Recorded on the tributary side, as the Chuzan dossier does.

region.text: control 'from Kuala Linggi to Kuala Kesang', roughly the modern state of Malacca

ledger.note: By 1424: Megat Iskandar Shah's control spreads along the Malacca coast. The page dates it only to his reign, 1414-1424; the year is the end of the reign. The Megat Iskandar Shah page (opened for this check) does not describe the extent of his control; it gives his death in 1424 and tribute to the Yongle Emperor in 1414. The Malacca page's wording, 'the Sultan's control spread from Kuala Linggi to Kuala Kesang', stays the only source and is undated within the reign.

region.text: Pahang, Ligor's vassal, conquered by a fleet under Bendahara Tun Perak

ledger.note: 1454: Malacca conquers Pahang. 'A fleet under Bendahara Tun Perak proceeded to Pahang and conquered it in 1454'; the last pre-Malaccan ruler Dewa Sura was taken to Malacca and Tun Hamzah governed Pahang.

region.text: 'the incorporation of territory between the Dindings and Johor'

ledger.note: By 1459: Muzaffar Shah's reign brings the west coast from the Dindings to Johor into the realm; he was 'the first Malaccan ruler to hold authority over both ends of the peninsula'. The page gives the reign (1446-1459), not a year; the year is the end of the reign. The Muzaffar Shah of Malacca page (opened for this check) gives the reign 1446-1459 and the 1456 Siamese plan but is silent on territory; the Malacca page's sentence is undated within the reign.

region.text: Pahang, conquered 1454, now a separate sultanate under a Malaccan prince

ledger.note: 1470: Pahang stops being governed directly from Malacca. Muhammad Shah, a Malaccan prince, 'was installed as sultan around 1470'; infobox 'Established: 1470'. The page gives 'around 1470', so the year is rounded.

region.text: the new Pahang sultanate, 'a vassal of Melaka'

ledger.note: 1470: Pahang becomes Malacca's vassal. Infobox 'Status: Vassal state of the Malacca Empire (1470-1511)'; the page says the sultanate 'has its origin as a vassal of Melaka'. The Alauddin Riayat Shah page calls Pahang 'a region under Malaccan rule' with Raja Ahmad as ruler (1477-1488); the Mansur Shah page says Pahang, Kampar and Indragiri 'unsuccessfully asserted their autonomy'.

region.text: Perak and Bernam, Manjung, Rupat, Singapore and Bintan, 'under Malacca's control during his rule' (Mansur Shah page)

ledger.note: By 1477: under Mansur Shah the Dindings coast, Perak and Bernam, Rupat, Singapore and Bintan are held. The Mansur Shah page, opened again, says 'Manjung, Rupat, Singapore, and Bintan, were under the control of Malacca during his rule' with no year; the year is the end of the reign (1459-1477). The Malacca Sultanate page says Perak 'was not conquered by Malacca' and was founded after 1528: the pages disagree.

region.text: Indragiri, Jambi, Tungkal and Siantan, handed over by Majapahit; Kampar added to the realm. Siak is not in this gain: it is drawn once, as a vassal

ledger.note: By 1477: Mansur Shah receives Indragiri, Jambi, Tungkal and Siantan when Majapahit's king 'agreed to marry off his daughter' to him (the Mansur Shah page names only Siantan and Indragiri as dowry). Kampar is added to the realm. No year is given on either page (the Indragiri Sultanate page could not be loaded, see notes); the year is the end of the reign. Siak was cut out of this gain: the Malacca page also says 'he later added Kampar and Siak to his realm', but the Mansur Shah page and the same page's other sentence call Siak a vassal, so the dossier draws Siak once, as a vassal (next event). Region coarse: Jambi is a province, Kampar a radius round Bangkinang, Indragiri a radius between Rengat and Tembilahan; Siantan lies in the Riau Islands and is covered by the 1488 event.

region.text: Siak in Sumatra (Siak Sri Indrapura on the Siak River, approximate)

ledger.note: By 1477: 'Mansur Shah was also able to vassalise Siak in Sumatra.' (Mansur Shah page: 'Siak became Malacca's vassal'.) No year on either page; the Siak Sultanate page, opened for this check, is silent on Malacca (it dates the later Siak sultanate to 1722). One status for Siak: the same Malacca page also says 'he later added Kampar and Siak to his realm', which is read as the looser wording; the circle is no longer inside the direct gain. Pahang, Kampar and Indragiri later asserted their autonomy 'but were eventually subdued'.

region.text: the Riau-Lingga islands

ledger.note: By 1488: Alauddin Riayat Shah 'extended the conquests of his father to include the Riau-Lingga islands'. No year; the year is the end of his reign (1477-1488). Terengganu and Rokan rulers paid homage; the page does not say they were conquered. The Alauddin Riayat Shah of Malacca page (opened for this check) gives the reign 1477-1488 and is silent on conquests.

region.text: Kelantan

ledger.note: 1506: Malacca conquers Kelantan. 'Malacca was still looking to expand its territory as late as 1506, when it conquered Kelantan.'

1511: Mahmud Shah withdraws from Malacca to a camp at the Muar River mouth, then (forced out in 1512) to Pahang as a guest, then to Bintan (infobox 'Bintan (1511-1526)'); the dossier puts the move to Bintan at 1513.

region.text: the hinterland of Malacca to the mouth of the Muar River

ledger.note: 1511: the sultan camps 'at the mouth of the Muar River' and waits for the Portuguese to leave; the page says only that 'in May' the Portuguese with over 2,000 local allies forced him out, and Albuquerque left in January 1512. The raids from Bintan continue until 1526.

region.text: Pahang, Malacca's vassal sultanate since 1470

ledger.note: 1511: Pahang ceases to be Malacca's vassal. Capture infobox: 'independence of Kampar, Pahang, and others'; Pahang page infobox: 'Vassal state of the Malacca Empire (1470-1511)'. The page adds that Pahang 'gradually grew independent', welcomed the fleeing sultan for about a year and sent troops to Malacca's defence in 1511, so the break is not sharp.

region.text: Kampar in Sumatra, approximate

ledger.note: 1511: Kampar becomes independent. Capture infobox 'independence of Kampar, Pahang, and others'; the text: 'the only renegade state recorded was Kampar, which provided the Portuguese with a local base'. Mahmud Shah came back to Kampar as a refuge in 1526 (see that year).

region.text: the rest of the realm: the peninsular and island provinces gained 1424-1506, apart from the Malacca-Muar zone the sultan still contested (drawn as the contest below)

ledger.note: 1511: the provinces do not follow the fallen sultan. The Capture infobox lists 'independence of Kampar, Pahang, and others' without naming the others; the Malacca page says the former vassals 'were no longer paying homage to him'; no page says any province stayed Malaccan, and Indragiri, which sent troops in 1511, is not said to have stayed. Read as: Melaka's countryside, Negeri Sembilan, Selangor, Johor, Perak, Kelantan, Singapore, the Riau Islands, Jambi and Indragiri leave in 1511. Some became states (Perak and Johor from 1528 under his sons); the rest are drawn as nobody's land.

region.text: Malacca's tributary relation to the Ming ends with the fall of the realm

ledger.note: 1511: the tribute to the Ming lapses with the fall. No page dates its end; Mahmud Shah's embassy to China from Pahang failed ('the Chinese merchants got there first and the ambassador got nothing for his trouble').

region.text: the city of Malacca

ledger.note: 1511: the Portuguese take Malacca. Albuquerque's second assault succeeded on 15 August 1511 (infobox; the Portuguese Malacca page says the city 'fell to the Portuguese on 24 August'); 'the city of Malacca remained under Portuguese control for the next 130 years'.

region.text: Siak in Sumatra (Siak Sri Indrapura on the Siak River, approximate)

ledger.note: 1511: the Siak tie is closed here by bridging: the Capture infobox gives 'independence of Kampar, Pahang, and others' without naming Siak, and the Malacca page says the former vassals 'were no longer paying homage' to Mahmud Shah after the fall. No page names Siak.

region.text: Bintan, 'an island kingdom ... that he usurped'

ledger.note: 1513: Mahmud Shah makes Bintan his base. 'Afterwards, Mahmud moved to Bintan, an island kingdom south-east of Singapore that he usurped to wage war on the Portuguese in Malacca.' The page gives no year; 1513 is the researcher's reading (about a year in Pahang after the camp fell in 1512; the Malacca infobox lists his second reign from 1513).
1513: Mahmud Shah's court settles on Bintan (infobox 'Bintan (1511-1526)'); the year is the researcher's reading.

region.text: the hinterland of Malacca to the mouth of the Muar River

ledger.note: 1526: the Portuguese 'devastated Bintan in 1526', ending the raids on Portuguese Malacca; the sultan retreats to Kampar.

region.text: Bintan, 'returning it to its previous ruler and making it a vassal'

ledger.note: 1526: the Portuguese raze Bintan and give it back to its previous ruler. Capture page: they 'devastated Bintan in 1526, returning it to its previous ruler and vassalizing the kingdom'. Counterpart is the Bintan kingdom, a Portuguese vassal from now (Portugal's own dossier should carry the vassal_start).
1526: Mahmud Shah retreats to Kampar, Sumatra, and rules in exile there.

region.text: Kampar in Sumatra, approximate

ledger.note: 1526: the exile court takes refuge in Kampar. 'Mahmud Shah then retreated to Kampar, Sumatra and led a government-in-exile there until he died in 1527.' The page does not say whether Kampar submitted or merely sheltered him.

region.text: the south: Alauddin Riayat Shah II 'established a new capital by the Johor River' (Johor Sultanate page)

ledger.note: 1528: Alauddin Riayat Shah II founds Johor. 'The Johor Sultanate was founded in 1528 by Sultan Alauddin Riayat Shah II (1528-1564) and was based at Pekan Tua.' A dynastic split, not a transfer of held land: since 1511 the exile court held only the Muar camp, Bintan and Kampar. Kepulauan Riau is no longer handed over (Bintan was returned to its previous ruler in 1526 and the other islands left in 1511); the islands and the Sumatran coast are Johor's later holdings ('at its height', Johor page).

region.text: the north of the peninsula

ledger.note: 1528: Muzaffar Shah is invited to rule Perak. The Perak page gives no year for the founding; the Malacca page puts the partition into Johor and Perak in 1528. Dynastic as well: Perak was not held by the exile court after 1511.

region.text: Kampar, the exile court's last ground, where Mahmud Shah died

ledger.note: 1528: Mahmud Shah dies at Kampar and the sultanate is partitioned into Johor and Perak (infobox 'Partition: 1528'); the Capture page gives his death as 1527. The shape that ends is the Kampar refuge; the pages do not say which heir took it.

wars.name: Ayutthaya invasions of Malacca
wars.outcome: Malacca repelled a land invasion in 1446, a sea attack in 1456 (its navy chased the Siamese back to Singapura) and an abortive invasion c. 1500 after Mahmud Shah rejected Ayutthaya's overlordship; no border moved.
wars.note: 'it launched a land invasion of Malacca in 1446'; 'In 1456, Ayutthaya launched another attack, this time by sea'; 1500 'the former resulting in an abortive invasion'.

wars.name: Malaccan conquest of Pahang
wars.outcome: Malacca conquered Pahang in 1454 and installed Tun Hamzah as governor.
wars.note: The campaign aimed 'to check Ligorian claims'; the expedition is credited to Raja Abdullah, Muzaffar Shah's son.

wars.name: Capture of Malacca (1511)
wars.outcome: Portuguese victory on 15 August 1511 (infobox; 24 August in the Portuguese Malacca text); the city stayed Portuguese for 130 years.
wars.note: First assault 25 July failed; further assault on 8 August; Albuquerque took 'full control of the city' on 24 August.

wars.name: Exiled sultan's war on Portuguese Malacca

zones.text: the hinterland of Malacca to the Muar River

wars.outcome: Raids and counter-raids from the Muar camp, Pahang and Bintan; the Portuguese razed Bintan in 1526 and the sultan withdrew to Kampar.
wars.note: Label is the researcher's: the page narrates the exile and Bintan's destruction without a war title. The Portuguese Malacca page lists a Battle of Muar River in 1523 (the Pahang page: Pahang supported 'Johor's attack on Melaka. Johor won at the Muar River', the exile court being called Johor in those sources) and Demak's failed fleets of 1511 and 1521.

certainty.note: A port polity whose reach is a list of coasts, islands and river mouths (Kuala Linggi to Kuala Kesang, the Dindings to Johor, Siak, Kampar, Riau-Lingga); no treaty line or survey exists, and after 1511 the exile court's real control is unknown.

sources.title: Muzaffar Shah of Malacca
sources.note: Opened for the thin Dindings-to-Johor coast: reign 1446-1459, silent on territory.

sources.title: Siak Sultanate
sources.note: Opened for the year Siak became a vassal: silent on Malacca; the Siak sultanate is of 1722.

sources.title: Alauddin Riayat Shah of Malacca
sources.note: Opened for the Riau-Lingga date: reign 1477-1488, silent on conquests; calls Pahang 'a region under Malaccan rule'.

notes:
Cliopatria row: 'Sultanate of Malacca' 1459-1861 is mostly wrong. The sultanate ended in 1528 (partition into Johor and Perak; Mahmud Shah died at Kampar), so the eleven shapes from 1529 to 1861 are verdict wrong; the town of Malacca was Portuguese 1511-1641, Dutch (VOC) 1641-1795 and 1818-1825, under British Residents 1795-1818, British from 1825. The 1459 shape (6,939 km2) lies on Singapore, south Johor and the Riau Islands, not on Malacca town. The 1512-1528 shape (230,357 km2) is replaced after review: the Capture page's infobox says 'independence of Kampar, Pahang, and others', so the exile court is drawn on what the page places the sultan on (the Muar camp 1512, Bintan 1513-1525, Kampar 1526-1528); every other province leaves in 1511 (ledger).
Founding is c. 1400 (infobox) while Cliopatria starts in 1459; two new keyframes cover 1400-1458.
Dates inside reigns (Muzaffar Shah, Mansur Shah, Alauddin Riayat Shah) are given at the reign's last year at confidence 1 because the pages give no year; the 1454 Pahang and 1506 Kelantan conquests are dated by the pages.
Disagreements: Mahmud Shah's death 1528 (Malacca, Perak pages) or 1527 (Capture page); Mansur Shah's reign start 1456 (his infobox) or 1459 (text); the fall of the city 15 August (infobox) or 24 August (Portuguese Malacca text); Perak was 'not conquered by Malacca' (Malacca page) yet 'brought under Malacca's control' (Mansur Shah page).
Not drawn: Malacca paid tribute to the Ming from 1405 with a promise of protection (Malacca page); that is Malacca's tribute, not Ming territory, and no vassal event is given. Cliopatria's Majapahit shape (1459-1474, 1.0 M km2) covers the Malacca Strait and contains the 1459 Malacca shape: a matter for the Majapahit dossier.
Counterparts that need dossiers: Pahang before 1454 (Ligor's vassal, Dewa Sura), Siak, Kampar, Indragiri, Kelantan before 1506. The Bintan site coordinates, 'Dindings' (Manjung) and 'Bintan' are not gazetteer names: used as a radius around 100.6 E 4.2 N and Tanjungpinang.
Repair pass (2026-10-19): Pahang leaves direct rule in 1470 and is a vassal sultanate to 1511; Siak is drawn once, as a vassal; Kampar and the other provinces are lost in 1511; Bintan is taken (1513, year unconfirmed) and lost (1526) to the Bintan kingdom; the 1528 split to Johor no longer hands on the Riau Islands; Singapura is listed as predecessor with no land passed; Malacca's Ming tribute is recorded (1405-1511). Pages opened again or for the first time: Megat Iskandar Shah, Muzaffar Shah of Malacca, Siak Sultanate, Alauddin Riayat Shah of Malacca (all silent on territory dates, so the confidence-1 gains of 1424, 1459, 1477 and 1488 stay at 1). Not loadable: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indragiri_Sultanate, https://id.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kesultanan_Indragiri, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kampar_Kingdom.
